sentence: A GP or nurse will ask questions and listen to the chest.
A simple breathing test may be used to check for signs of asthma, and sometimes a blood test.
Specific tests include FeNO, spirometry and peak flow testing.

sentence: Spirometry measures how much air a person can blow out and how fast.
Peak flow testing records how fast a person can blow air out, usually at home over a period of time.

sentence: UK guidance for adults and young people starts with blood eosinophils or a FeNO test.
If asthma is not confirmed that way, the next step is spirometry with a bronchodilator reversibility test.
Peak flow readings over time are used when spirometry is unavailable or delayed.
For children aged 5 to 16, FeNO comes first, followed by spirometry.

sentence: Inhalers are the main treatment for asthma.
Reliever inhalers are used to treat symptoms when they occur, while preventer inhalers are taken daily.
A preventer reduces inflammation in the airways.
note: Summary of Asthma + Lung UK pages

sentence: A reliever does not treat the asthma itself, only the symptoms it causes.

sentence: The latest guidelines do not recommend giving anyone with asthma only a blue reliever inhaler.
Anyone who has only a reliever should also have a steroid preventer.
The NHS says tablets and other treatments may be needed if asthma is severe.

sentence: Serious allergic reactions to these medicines are rare but can be life-threatening.

sentence: Repeated or continuous courses of steroid tablets are linked to complications such as fractures from thin bones and pneumonia.

sentence: Living with severe asthma is linked to some risks, including a lower life expectancy in one source.
The NHS describes an asthma attack as severe symptoms and difficulty breathing, which can be life-threatening.
The NHS advises sitting up straight and trying to keep calm while taking puffs of the reliever inhaler.
It says to call 999 if symptoms get worse at any point, do not improve after the maximum reliever dose, or there is no inhaler.
NHS inform says to call 999 or go to A&E for severe breathing difficulty, such as struggling to speak without pausing.

NHS 111 Wales adds that 999 is needed if a person is too breathless to speak, eat or sleep, or the reliever is not helping.
If symptoms settle and 999 is not needed, the advice is still to see a GP or asthma nurse soon.
